paper_title: PAD: Policy-Aware Data Valuation for Autonomous Driving

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: End-to-end autonomous driving increasingly depends on scaling training demonstrations, yet data growth does not guarantee proportional gains. However, additional data do not guarantee better policies: a demonstration that benefits one planner may be redundant or harmful to another. Existing curation methods typically infer data value from intrinsic sample properties or training-dependent proxies that do not measure downstream policy utility. To address this, we introduce \textbf{Policy-Aware Data Valuation (PAD)}, a framework that assigns each candidate demonstration a utility specific to the target driving policy. PAD combines scene-level calibration feedback with projected policy gradients and a regularized approximation of local training geometry, producing scalable influence-based values for the policy. A controlled group-removal study establishes the directional fidelity of these values, while cross-planner analysis shows that the same candidate pool induces markedly different rankings across planner families. On DiffusionDrive, PAD improves EPDMS over real-only training by $3.5$ points on NavTest and $5.0$ points on NavHard. Policy-specific curation consistently outperforms real-only and full-pool training across diffusion-, regression-, and flow-matching-based planners while substantially reducing scene-level regressions. These results establish policy-aware data valuation as a basis for replacing indiscriminate data accumulation with targeted policy improvement, enabling more efficient and reliable scaling of autonomous-driving systems.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content: End-to-end autonomous driving has advanced rapidly through increasingly capable policy architectures (Zheng et al. 2024; Chen et al. 2024), yet attainable performance remains constrained by the quality and composition of their training data (Feng et al. 2026). The success of large-scale vision and language models has consequently motivated the continued expansion of real and synthetic driving corpora (Jiang et al. 2025). Data volume, however, does not translate predictably into policy improvement. Additional demonstrations may be redundant, inconsistent with the learning objective, or harmful because of distribution and supervision errors (Shumailov et al. 2024; Jiao et al. 2026; Atakishiyev, Salameh, Corresponding author. and Goebel 2025). Such data can produce diminishing returns and scenario-specific regressions even when aggregate performance improves. The central data problem is therefore not simply how much to collect, but which demonstrations improve given driving policy (Dimlioglu et al. 2026; Xu et al. 2026a). Addressing this problem requires policy-dependent definition of data value. Research on data attribution and modelaware filtering increasingly evaluates training samples through their effects on learned models (Yu, Das, and Xiong 2024; Guo et al. 2026). This perspective reveals that demonstration has no policy-independent utility. The same sample may reinforce useful behavior in one policy while exerting negligible or adverse influence in another (Choe et al. 2026; Hammoudeh and Lowd 2024). We accordingly define policyaware data valuation as estimating the downstream utility of an individual demonstration with respect to the target policy that learns from it. Existing driving-data construction and curation methods capture only part of this policy dependence. Datasetgeneration methods expand scale and coverage, usually treating complex or challenging scenarios as inherently valuable (Rowe et al. 2025; Xiao et al. 2025). Data-intrinsic heuristics similarly prioritize rarity, diversity, or difficulty without measuring downstream learning effects (Jiao et al. 2026). However, scenario complexity is not equivalent to training utility and cannot reflect whether demonstration induces beneficial update for particular policy. Trainingdependent signals such as loss, uncertainty, and gradient salience reflect the current policy but need not correspond to downstream driving performance (Luo et al. 2026; Wang et al. 2024a). Datasetor cluster-level filtering can further conceal substantial variation among demonstrations within the same group (Calian et al. 2026; Chhabra et al. 2025). The unresolved challenge is scalable, per-demonstration estimator that connects candidates effect on policy optimization to its downstream utility. To address this challenge, Policy-Aware Data Valuation (PAD) is introduced. As illustrated in Fig. 1, PAD evaluates target policy on an independent calibration set and uses the resulting scene-level outcomes to weight gradients of its native training objective. Projected gradients and regularized approximation of local training geometry then yield policy-specific value for each candidate demonstration, which Figure 1: Overview of PAD, which combines scene-level advantages from an independent calibration split with projected planning gradients and local training geometry to estimate the planner-relative influence of each demonstration, enabling budgeted selection of beneficial data for retraining. supports budgeted selection for retraining. Controlled removal experiments show that these values predict realized training effects, while cross-policy analysis reveals distinct valuations of the same candidate pool. On DiffusionDrive, PAD improves EPDMS over real-only training by 3.5 points on NavTest and 5.0 points on NavHard, with consistent gains across multiple policy families and fewer scene-level regressions. Our contributions are summarized as follows: Policy-aware data valuation. We formulate the value of each driving demonstration relative to the target policy and its downstream utility, rather than as an intrinsic property of the sample. Scalable per-demonstration estimation. We develop an influence-based estimator that integrates scene-level policy outcomes, projected training gradients, and regularized local geometry within unified interface across policy families. Comprehensive empirical validation. We show that PAD predicts realized training effects, produces distinct valuations across policies, improves downstream driving performance, and reduces scene-level regression exposure.

2.1 Driving Data Construction and Curation
End-to-end driving systems increasingly rely on large and
heterogeneous training corpora (Zhou et al. 2026; Kirby et al.
2026; Xu et al. 2025). Real-world fleet collection provides
authentic driving behavior but remains costly, geographically
constrained, and inherently sparse in safety-critical events (Liu
et al. 2025; Wang et al. 2024b). Simulation and synthetic-data
generation complement this process by expanding scenario
coverage and enabling targeted construction of rare, interac-
tive, or challenging situations (Jiang et al. 2024; Rowe et al.
2025; Kim et al. 2025). These approaches have broadened the
demonstrations available to driving models, but their primary
sections.content: objective is to construct the candidate data pool rather than determine how an individual demonstration will affect the policy trained on it. As driving datasets grow, data curation methods seek to prioritize demonstrations according to intrinsic properties such as rarity, coverage or difficulty through sample selection, clustering, or reweighting (Lu et al. 2026; Embacher et al. 2026). Most of these methods implicitly regard complex or challenging scenarios as especially valuable (Xiao et al. 2025). Although such criteria are useful for improving dataset composition, scenario complexity is not equivalent to training utility (Xu et al. 2026b). difficult demonstration may be redundant or harmful under imperfect supervision, while an ordinary demonstration may correct consequential policy deficiency (Ge et al. 2025). Data-intrinsic criteria therefore characterize the demonstration itself but cannot establish its downstream contribution to target policy.

sections.title: 2.2 Training Data Valuation
sections.content: Learner-aware curation methods address this limitation by evaluating samples through training-dependent signals, including loss, uncertainty, and gradient statistics (Wang et al. 2024a; Xia et al. 2024). These signals reflect the state of the model, but they typically quantify difficulty, confidence, or optimization salience rather than the effect of sample on the downstream objective of interest (Mlodozeniec et al. 2026). Training data attribution provides more direct counterfactual formulation by asking how perturbing or removing an individual example changes target model behavior (Ye et al. 2025). Though these methods offer an empirical estimate of this effect, they can be prohibitively expensive at scale, especially in autonomous driving systems. Instead, influence functions and scalable gradient-based approximations estimate the response of target quantity to infinitesimal changes in sample weight without retraining for every candidate, thereby defining data value relative to both learner and an evaluation objective (Tan et al. 2026; Agia et al. 2025). Training data attribution has supported dataset debugging, behavior tracing, and data selection in supervised learning and large models (Dass et al. 2025; Bae et al. 2024), and has recently been applied to robot demonstrations (Agia et al. 2025). Per-demonstration valuation remains underexplored in autonomous driving, where high-dimensional sensory policies complicate attribution and supervised training losses do not directly represent downstream driving utility. Existing driving-data methods consequently rely largely on proxy scores or coarse-grained groups, leaving the planning effect of individual demonstrations unresolved (Ruan et al. 2026). In this paper, the proposed PAD addresses this gap by combining independent scene-level policy outcomes with scalable projected influence estimation to assign policy-specific values to individual driving demonstrations.

sections.title: 5 Conclusion
sections.content: This paper introduced PAD, policy-aware framework that defines the value of driving demonstration by its downstream utility to the policy that learns from it. By combining independent scene-level policy outcomes with projected training gradients and regularized local geometry, PAD converts otherwise intractable retraining effects into scalable per-demonstration valuations. The results show that these values track realized training effects and enable policy-specific curation that consistently improves driving performance across distinct policy families while substantially reducing scene-level regression exposure. These findings establish that data utility is inherently policy dependent and that effective scaling requires optimizing data composition rather than volume alone. The current study is limited by its local first-order approximation and its evaluation on synthetic candidates within NAVSIM. Future work will model training-stage dependence and higherorder interactions, and extend validation to heterogeneous real-world data and broader closed-loop conditions.
